proof:
Small coefficient variations retain an interior ball at each of the finitely many sites by strict slack. Boundedness of any old fiber gives a positive minimum of $\max_f n_f\cdot y$ on the unit sphere, which persists and bounds the changed fibers since their thresholds at the finite sites remain bounded. Work in a bounded ball that strictly contains the perturbed fibers. For a fixed direction, changes of indicators can occur only in strips of width $O(t)$ about the original finitely many body or cap hyperplanes. At a point in the relative interior of a facet, all rows outside its owner list have strict slack. Along the normal line through the point, the first-order displacement for owner $f$ is $tr_f$, since its original continuous normal is the unit outward facet normal. The intersection of the owner inequalities therefore moves at first-order speed $r=\min_{f\in O(z,F)}r_f$. Away from a coincident facet, the cap contributes this same speed on the strictly inside portion, zero on the strictly outside portion, and on its proper section it sweeps with first-order speed $\tau_j$ in the direction outward from the cap.

For precision, in the normal coordinates of each distinct hyperplane omit a fixed $\varepsilon$-neighborhood within that hyperplane of the lower-dimensional faces and of its intersections with the other nonparallel hyperplanes. On the remaining compact pieces the relevant strict inequalities are uniform, so the linear displacement formulas give the strip integrals after dividing by $t$ and letting $t\downarrow0$. Parallel distinct hyperplanes are a fixed distance apart. The omitted part has $(d-1)$-area $O(\varepsilon)$ in the bounded ball and lies in strips of thickness $O(t)$, so its contribution after division by $t$ is $O(\varepsilon)$ uniformly for small $t$. Sending $\varepsilon$ to zero proves the claimed integrations and discards lower-dimensional contact. Coincident hyperplanes are considered together, and in dimension one distinct boundary points are separated with no lower-dimensional exception.

On a coincident facet, use the normal coordinate for which the cap is the upper side. If the body lies in the cap, the lower body boundary moves by $-tr$ and the lower cap boundary by $-t\tau_j$, so the volume derivative density is $\min(r,\tau_j)$. Choose either one minimizing owner or the cap branch. Their convex allocations are exactly $\sum_f\alpha_{jf}+\sigma_j=1$. If the body lies on the opposite side, its upper boundary moves by $tr$, and the cap's lower boundary by $-t\tau_j$. The retained layer has derivative density $\max(r+\tau_j,0)$. Choose either one minimizing owner together with the full section weight, or zero weights for both. The resulting convex family is exactly $\sum_f\alpha_{jf}=\sigma_j\in[0,1]$. On every facet, choices of a minimizing owner and subsequent branches may use first-index tie breaking, which is measurable. This realizes the objective minimum and puts each cap's derivative among its indicated linear evaluations, giving the asserted upper bound.

Finally regard the weights as positive measures dominated by the fixed finite facet measures. The inequalities and partition relations are weakly closed on those compact facets, and domination gives weak compactness. Each covector uses only masses and first moments, continuous for this convergence. Taking their finite-dimensional images proves compactness and convexity.

statement:
Let finitely many positive compact polytopal fibers $K_z$ be represented by the same nonvertical ambient inequality list $n_f\cdot x+a_f\cdot z\le b_f$, with each $n_f$ initially unit. Also fix a nonvertical ambient cap with margin $v_j\cdot z+u_j\cdot x-b_j$ and initially unit $u_j$. In a joint coefficient direction write $r_f=\delta b_f-\delta a_f\cdot z-\delta n_f\cdot x$ and $\tau_j=\delta v_j\cdot z+\delta u_j\cdot x-\delta b_j$. For a fiber facet $F$, let $O(z,F)$ be its owners, the rows whose equality supports $F$. The one-sided total volume derivative is
$$
M'(\delta)=\min_{g\in G_0}g(\delta),\qquad
G_0=\left\{\delta\mapsto\sum_{z,F}\int_F\sum_{f\in O(z,F)}\omega_f r_f\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}:\ \omega_f\ge0,\ \sum_f\omega_f=1\right\}.
$$
All allocations are measurable. For each cap the one-sided derivative is at most $\max_{g\in G_j}g(\delta)$, where the compact convex set $G_j$ consists of
$$
\delta\mapsto \sum_{z,F}\int_F\sum_{f\in O(z,F)}\alpha_{jf}r_f\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}
 +\sum_z\int \tau_j\,d\nu_{jz}.
$$
On a facet portion strictly inside the cap, $\alpha_{jf}\ge0$ sum to one, and strictly outside they vanish. A proper cap section contributes ordinary $(d-1)$-area to $\nu_{jz}$, and strict full, strict empty and lower-dimensional contact sections contribute zero. On a coincident facet $F$, the section measure is $\sigma_j\mathcal H^{d-1}|_F$ from the same allocation as the body term. If the body lies inside the cap, $\alpha_{jf},\sigma_j\ge0$ and $\sum_f\alpha_{jf}+\sigma_j=1$. If it lies outside, $\alpha_{jf}\ge0$ and $\sum_f\alpha_{jf}=\sigma_j\in[0,1]$. Use counting measure on endpoints and proper sections when $d=1$.
title: One-sided volume and cap derivatives with shared-plane ownership
